one_liner: MIT C/C++ library of hand-vectorized image kernels (conversion, resize, filters) for x86 and Arm; no published win over OpenCV or libyuv.
what_it_does: A large C API (SimdLib.h, about 380 exported declarations) plus C++ wrappers (SimdLib.hpp, Simd::View) and a ctypes Python wrapper covering pixel-format conversion (BGR/BGRA/Gray/YUV/Bayer/HSV), resizing, filters, statistics, motion detection and the Synet neural-network kernels. Resizing is a context API: SimdResizerInit(srcX, srcY, dstX, dstY, channels, type, method) then SimdResizerRun, with nearest, bilinear (Simd, Caffe, PyTorch and OpenCV-compatible coordinate mappings), bicubic, area and area-fast methods. It is not a drop-in for OpenCV: images go through Simd::View, though defining SIMD_OPENCV_ENABLE adds cv::Mat <-> Simd::View conversion.
how_it_is_fast: Each function has a scalar Base version plus hand-written intrinsics versions for SSE4.1, AVX2, AVX-512BW, AVX-512VNNI and AMX-BF16 on x86 and NEON and SVE2 on Arm, each compiled in its own translation unit with matching -m flags, and SimdLib.cpp picks the best one at runtime from CPUID. Byte resizers use fixed-point interpolation, and the BilinearOpenCv mode reproduces OpenCV's integer arithmetic so output matches cv::resize within 1 level.
when_to_use: You need many pixel-level kernels (colour conversion, YUV planar conversions, reduce/stretch, statistics, motion-detection primitives) behind one MIT C API with runtime ISA dispatch, and do not want OpenCV's footprint.
Single-threaded per-frame processing on known x86 (AVX2/AVX-512) or Arm NEON hardware where you will benchmark against your current OpenCV build yourself.
You need bilinear resize that matches OpenCV output (SimdResizeMethodBilinearOpenCv) or PyTorch/Caffe coordinate mappings for neural-network preprocessing.
Embedded or plugin builds that need a static library with no external dependencies.
when_not_to_use: As a proven speedup over OpenCV: two user reports (issue #149: upscale 3328x1032 to 3752x1080, Simd 9.789 ms vs OpenCV 4.5.1 3.689 ms on an i7-10700; issue #212: Simd::Resize and Simd::BgrToGray '4-6 times slower than OpenCV4.5.5' on an i7-10750H) went unanswered and no counter-benchmark is published.

Multi-core throughput on large images: SimdGetThreadNumber defaults to 1 and only some functions (GEMM, Synet layers, ResizerNearest since 2025) are parallelized, while OpenCV and libyuv callers usually get threading or IPP for free.
High-quality resampling: there is no Lanczos or other windowed-sinc filter; use fast_image_resize or Pillow-SIMD class libraries for that.

Projects that need a stable API: release 8.0.166 (2026-10-01) removed SimdFill, SimdFillBgr, SimdFillBgra, SimdCopyFrame, the HOG, Neural, HAAR/LBP Detection and 8-bit Synet functions and dropped RISC-V and Hexagon HVX support; major versions moved 6 to 7 to 8 within 2026.
macOS or other non-Windows/Linux targets: the README lists only 32/64-bit Windows and Linux.

integration.form: static lib (default with CMake; DLL by default in the MSVS 2022 project; SIMD_SHARED for a shared lib)
integration.dependencies: none (OpenCV optional, test framework only); vcpkg port 'simd'
integration.min_toolchain: C++11 (-std=c++11), CMake 3.10, GCC/Clang or MSVS 2022; AVX-512BW TUs need GCC 5.5+, VNNI GCC 8+, AMX GCC 11+ with binutils 2.34+
integration.platforms: x86 and x86-64 (scalar, SSE4.1, AVX2, AVX-512BW, AVX-512VNNI, AMX-BF16 runtime-dispatched), ARM32/aarch64 NEON, SVE/SVE2 (off by default); Windows and Linux
integration.thread_safety: not documented; resizer and filter contexts are const at run time and reusable for same-geometry images; SimdSetThreadNumber is a global setting

gotchas: Harness: the only OpenCV comparison in the repo, ResizeOpenCvSpecialTest in src/Test/TestResize.cpp, is fair in shape (cv::setNumThreads matched to SimdGetThreadNumber, random BGR24 480x640 to 333x444, both sides rebuild their tables per call since Simd::Resize does Init/Run/Release each time) but runs only with -DSIMD_OPENCV=ON and -m=s and no output is committed; the default -m=a mode only compares Simd's own scalar and SIMD versions.

The CMake build compiles the dispatcher SimdLib.cpp with -mavx2 -mfma (plus -mavx512bw on Unix when SIMD_AVX512 is ON), and the test app built with SIMD_TARGET set uses the same flags; illegal-instruction reports on older CPUs recur (#71 and #125 closed, #274 open on an Atom Z3735F).

Memory-safety bugs in SIMD paths are still being found: #299 (STITCH fuzzer with AddressSanitizer) was a 16-byte heap-buffer-overflow write in Avx512bw::TransformImageTranspose_4x4x16 for a 32x4 BGRA image rotated 270 degrees, and #333 (2026-04-09, open) reports a crash in Avx2::AbsDifferenceSums3x3AutoTest.

Not every method supports every channel type: OpenCV-bilinear, bicubic and area resizers are byte-only, Caffe/PyTorch bilinear are float/BF16-only, and SimdResizerInit returns NULL for unsupported combinations (the C++ Simd::Resize then hits assert(0), which is a no-op in release builds).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Simd over CompV, DeltaCV or KLERP when you need one maintained MIT library spanning conversion, resize and filters with AVX-512/AMX and SVE2 dispatch; for YUV conversion prefer libyuv or the measured sparkyuv/xxYUV, and for quality resampling prefer fast_image_resize or Pillow-SIMD, all of which publish numbers Simd lacks.
verified_claims_summary: No first-party numbers against OpenCV or libyuv exist; the repo's test mode only times Simd's scalar versus SIMD implementations. The only third-party figures found point the other way for resize and BgrToGray (issues #149 and #212, OpenCV 4.5.x 2.65x to 4-6x faster, thread counts unstated), while fwessels/go-cv-simd, a c2goasm Go port of Simd's SSE2 code, reports 3x3 Gaussian, mean and median filters 61-85% faster than OpenCV 2.x cvSmooth via go-opencv (filters only, OpenCV 2.x legacy C API, uninitialised images, hardware and image size not stated in the README).
status_note: Very active (monthly releases, 8.0.166 on 2026-10-01, about 5,950 commits, 2.3k stars, vcpkg port) and MIT-licensed, but the public API is pruned between major versions and the speed advantage over OpenCV is unmeasured, so treat it as tier D and benchmark against your own OpenCV build before switching.
